questions.q: Why is a model's in-sample AIC/BIC not sufficient evidence that it will forecast well?
options: AIC and BIC are only defined for AR models, not ARIMA
In-sample metrics are computed on the same data used to estimate the parameters and can reflect overfitting rather than genuine forecasting skill
AIC and BIC always equal zero for a well-specified model
In-sample metrics cannot be computed in statsmodels
questions.explain: In-sample fit statistics are computed on the training data itself, so a model can achieve a good AIC/BIC by fitting noise specific to that sample, which does not guarantee it forecasts new data well.

questions.q: What is the defining feature of walk-forward (rolling-origin) validation for time series?
options: Randomly shuffling the data into train and test sets
Fitting once on the full dataset and testing on the same data
Repeatedly fitting on data up to time T, forecasting just past T, then moving T forward and repeating
Using only the first 10% of the data for both fitting and testing
questions.explain: Walk-forward validation respects the time order of the data: it fits using only information available up to a given point, forecasts just beyond it, then advances the origin and repeats, simulating real production use.

questions.q: Which error metric is most sensitive to a few very large forecast errors, compared to the others?
options: MAE
MAPE
RMSE
All three are equally sensitive to large errors
questions.explain: RMSE squares each error before averaging, which disproportionately amplifies the effect of large errors compared to MAE's simple absolute value or MAPE's percentage framing.

questions.q: A fitted ARIMA model has a lower in-sample AIC than a naive random-walk 'forecast,' but a higher out-of-sample RMSE. What should you conclude?
options: The ARIMA model is better because AIC is the only metric that matters
The ARIMA model is failing to add real forecasting value relative to the simple naive benchmark, despite looking better in-sample
RMSE is not a valid metric for financial data
The naive forecast cannot be used as a benchmark
questions.explain: The naive random-walk benchmark is the standard the model must beat out-of-sample. A better in-sample AIC combined with worse out-of-sample error is a classic sign that the fitted model isn't actually forecasting better than doing almost nothing.

questions.q: Why can MAPE become unstable or undefined when applied to something like daily log returns?
options: MAPE requires exactly 252 trading days of data
MAPE divides each error by the actual value, which causes problems when actual values are near zero
MAPE can only be computed for seasonal models
MAPE is identical to RMSE by definition
questions.explain: MAPE's formula divides the absolute error by the actual value. When actual values (like daily returns) are frequently near zero, this division produces extremely large or undefined percentage errors.
